native_result.query: In what centuries did we see the highest growth phase of the period between 2000 BCE and 1100 BCE?
native_result.HypoA: Between 1500 BCE and 1300 BCE, highest growth of the period between 2000 BCE and 1100 BCE is seen.
native_result.HypoB: The highest growth phase between 2000 BCE and 1100 BCE occurred in the 15th–14th centuries BCE (~1500–1301 BCE), with the fastest growth in 1500–1400 BCE. Both dataset-provided growth-rate indicators — aggregate KDE growth rate (g_all_mean) and the percentage change of the 100-year-smoothed pollen openness score (pollen_grate_100) — peak in the 15th century BCE (1500–1401 BCE), with the 14th century BCE (1400–1301 BCE) second; level-based increases in KDE density and pollen openness are largest in the 14th century BCE, and capital-indicator Z-value changes support the same window. Growth turns negative by the 13th–12th centuries BCE (minimum 1200–1101 BCE). Assumes pollen PC1 openness is a demographic/human-impact proxy (higher openness = more human impact).
native_result.WorkflowB: Loaded the three staged CSVs (comma-decimal parsing for capital/pollen files); aligned all on annual CE (calBP = 1950 − CE verified); filtered 2000–1100 BCE (901 rows); computed century-bin means of primary rate columns g_all_mean and pollen_grate_100 plus their rank-average; computed century-to-century absolute level changes for kde_all_mean, pollen_inter_100, SMOOTH_MEAN_100y (secondary) and for capital.csv Z-indicators (tertiary, absolute change only, no % change); ran sensitivity checks: 100-year rolling windows (step 50), adjacent-century peak distinguishability using g_all_std standard errors, and exclusion of the single-year 1100 BCE boundary bin.
